clinical_knowledge.topic: Post-Stroke Spastic Hemiplegia evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Post-Stroke Spastic Hemiplegia is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes a stepwise spasticity program (stretching/splinting, then oral or focal botulinum toxin therapy) to prevent contracture, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: stiff, tight clenching of elbow/wrist and spastic catch on passive stretch with scissoring gait 6 months after MCA ischemic stroke

Key HPI features: 62F presenting 6 months after a middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke with progressive stiff, tight clenching of the elbow and wrist, a spastic catch on passive stretch, and a scissoring gait pattern.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals normal. Modified Ashworth Scale 3 spasticity in the affected upper extremity with flexor synergy posturing (elbow, wrist, and finger flexion) and a velocity-dependent catch on passive stretch. Lower extremity shows an extensor pattern with plantarflexion and a scissoring gait. Skin intact in palmar creases. Mild passive range-of-motion limitation at the elbow and wrist without fixed bony contracture.
Relevant background/PMH: Middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke 6 months ago with residual hemiplegia
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Post-Stroke Spastic Hemiplegia.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Parkinsonian rigidity without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe flexor contractures.
management_principles: Initiate regular stretching and range-of-motion exercises with resting hand/wrist splinting to prevent contracture
Consider oral antispasmodic agents (e.g., baclofen, tizanidine) for generalized spasticity
Use ultrasound- or EMG-guided botulinum toxin A injection for focal, functionally limiting spasticity in specific muscle groups
Monitor for skin breakdown in palmar creases and painful spasms, and refer for orthopedic evaluation if a fixed contracture develops despite treatment.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 62F presenting 6 months after a middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke with progressive stiff, tight clenching of the elbow and wrist, a spastic catch on passive stretch, and a scissoring gait pattern.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals normal. Modified Ashworth Scale 3 spasticity in the affected upper extremity with flexor synergy posturing and a velocity-dependent catch on passive stretch. Lower extremity shows an extensor pattern with plantarflexion and a scissoring gait. Skin intact in palmar creases. Mild passive range-of-motion limitation without fixed bony contracture.
reference_soap.assessment: Post-stroke spastic hemiplegia (upper motor neuron spasticity), Modified Ashworth Scale 3, with functional limitation and early risk of fixed contracture.
reference_soap.plan: Initiate a structured spasticity program: stretching/range-of-motion exercises and resting hand/wrist splinting, with physical/occupational therapy. Consider oral antispasmodics for generalized spasticity and ultrasound- or EMG-guided botulinum toxin A injection for focal, functionally limiting spasticity. Monitor for skin breakdown and reassess Modified Ashworth Scale and functional goals regularly.

must_ask.say: Does your arm or leg feel tight and snap back when you try to straighten it quickly?

must_ask.objective: Functional impact on hygiene and dressing
must_ask.say: Does the stiffness interfere with washing your palm or putting on clothes?
Do you experience sudden, painful muscle spasms in your leg at night?
Are you taking medications like baclofen or have you received Botox injections?
When did your stroke occur and how has the stiffness progressed since then?
